overview.intro: Sovereignty is the concept that does the heaviest work in political theory and international law: it identifies where final authority lies within a territory and which powers answer to no superior outside it. This unit examines its meaning and kinds, its characteristics, the historical analysis of how the idea took its modern shape, Austin’s command theory as its classical statement, and the pluralist challenge that denied sovereignty could be located in a single body at all.

facts.label: Kinds
facts.value: Internal sovereignty — supreme authority within the territory; external sovereignty — independence in international relations.

facts.label: Characteristics
facts.value: Supreme, final, indivisible, inalienable and absolute within its sphere.

facts.label: Austin

facts.label: Pluralists

learningOutcomes: Define sovereignty and distinguish its internal and external kinds.
Explain the historical development of the concept.
Account for Austin’s theory of sovereignty and its criticisms.
Explain the pluralist view and assess the debate.

blocks.text: Sovereignty is the supreme, independent and enduring authority of a State over its territory and inhabitants. Internal sovereignty concerns the locus of final authority inside the borders: some person or body must have the last word in law, and whoever has it can settle any dispute that arises within the order. External sovereignty concerns the State’s standing outside: in international law the State is equal to other States and subject to no superior except those obligations it has itself accepted by treaty or custom. The two kinds usually travel together, which is why they are easy to confuse, but they come apart in colonial rule, in protectorates and in federations, where internal authority is qualified while external recognition persists or vice versa.

items: Sovereignty is a property of the State, not of any single organ within it.
Internal sovereignty is about finality of decision; external is about independence.
Treaty obligations are accepted limits and therefore do not contradict external sovereignty.
Recognition by other States is the practical evidence of external sovereignty.

blocks.text: Sovereignty is usually described by five characteristics. It is supreme, because no other authority within the territory stands above it in law; final, because it settles disputes that lower authorities cannot; indivisible, because power shared to the point of rival sovereigns is not sovereignty at all; inalienable, because it cannot be given away without the State ceasing to be what it was; and absolute within its sphere, meaning that no positive law limits it from outside, whatever limits morality, prudence or its own constitution may impose.

The idea itself has a history. In medieval Europe political authority was divided and layered: the emperor and the pope claimed universal jurisdiction, kings were constrained by charter, fief and custom, and no single will was acknowledged as final. The modern doctrine emerged from the religious wars, when the need for an authority that could end the conflict produced Bodin’s definition of sovereignty as the absolute and perpetual power of a commonwealth, and Hobbes’s Leviathan carried it further. The nation-state, the decline of transnational claims and the doctrine of non-intervention consolidated it in international practice, while the twentieth century both extended it, through decolonisation, and qualified it, through human rights law and supranational unions. Understanding the history matters because it shows sovereignty as a historical achievement rather than a self-evident fact.

blocks.text: Austin offered the classical analytical statement. In every political society there must be a sovereign — a determinate human superior who is not habitually obeyed by any other like superior, and whom the bulk of the society obeys habitually and from fear of default. The sovereign is set apart by three marks: he receives habitual obedience from the bulk of the society; he is not habitually obedient to any other; and if he is a body, the members are incapable of acting under separate instructions. Commands backed by sanctions are law, and the sovereign, being the source of commands, is neither legally bound nor limited by them.

The criticisms are decisive in most later writing. The theory works best for a simple despotism and poorly for the cases that matter: in a federation sovereignty appears divided between the centre and the units, since each is supreme within its sphere; in constitutional monarchies the sovereign in law, the monarch, does not govern, so sovereignty lies with an institution that exercises none of the powers attributed to it; in parliamentary systems sovereignty in the crown-in-parliament is not the habitual obedience of individuals to a determinate person but a legal fiction about an abstract body. The habit of obedience is also an inadequate criterion, since subjects obey magistrates, employers and customs as well as the supposed sovereign, and where custom binds a state, as in Britain’s constitution, the sovereign is bound in substance even while sovereign in form. Austin’s defenders reply that he was offering an analytical standard rather than a description of every polity, and that the question of where final authority lies still has to be answered somewhere.

learn.title: The pluralist view and the assessment of the debate

blocks.text: The pluralists denied that sovereignty could be found at all in the modern state. Figgis argued that a church or a voluntary association has its own life and purpose which the state cannot confer or revoke, and that the doctrine of parliamentary sovereignty was a legal claim about courts rather than a sociological fact about power. Laski held that obligation is relative to the function performed, so the individual owes duties to the state, the profession, the trade union and the family in varying degrees, and no single relationship is absolute. Dicey, from inside the legal tradition, distinguished the sovereignty of law from the sovereignty of persons, arguing that in Britain the will expressed is not the will of a monarch but of the legislature, which is itself subject to the conventions and opinions that sustain it.

The unitary reply is that pluralism confuses the sources of influence with the location of authority. Many bodies may shape decisions, but in the last resort someone must be able to settle the question finally, and the state retains the power to tax, to legislate, to conscript and to enforce judgments, which no association can match. The best modern position holds that sovereignty remains a useful concept provided it is understood as legal finality rather than as unlimited power: states can be legally supreme internally while accepting treaty obligations externally, and domestic constitutional limits constrain government in practice without transferring sovereignty elsewhere. The debate therefore ends not with the abolition of the concept but with a narrower and more defensible version of it.

questions.explanation: Related to indivisibility: authority that is given away entirely is no longer supreme authority.

questions.prompt: The sixteenth-century writer who defined sovereignty as the absolute and perpetual power of a commonwealth was __________ .
questions.explanation: His formulation supplied the modern doctrine as it was later developed by Hobbes.

questions.answer: Sovereignty is supreme, since no authority stands above it in law; final, because it settles disputes that lower bodies cannot; indivisible, because shared to the point of rival sovereigns it ceases to exist; and inalienable, because it cannot be given away without the State losing its character. It is also absolute within its sphere, meaning that no positive law imposed from outside limits it, though the State’s own constitution and law may.
questions.explanation: All five characteristics should be named with a short explanation of each.

questions.prompt: Explain three objections to Austin’s theory of sovereignty.
questions.answer: The first objection is constitutional: in a constitutional monarchy the sovereign in law, the monarch, does not govern, so the body identified as sovereign exercises none of the powers the theory attributes to it, and real authority lies with a legislature and ministries the theory cannot fit. The second is federal: where the constitution distributes subjects between the centre and the units, each is supreme within its own sphere, so sovereignty appears divided exactly where Austin insists it must be single. The third is customary and social: subjects obey custom, law, employers and institutions as well as political commands, so habitual obedience to a determinate superior is not the fact it is claimed to be, and much law that binds states is not a command backed by sanction at all. The objection that the sovereign is in substance limited by constitution and opinion may also be given.
questions.explanation: Three objections must each name the case that defeats the criterion it attacks.

questions.prompt: Explain the meaning and characteristics of sovereignty, distinguishing its internal and external kinds.
questions.answer: Sovereignty is the supreme, independent and enduring authority of a State, and it exists in two distinguishable kinds. Internal sovereignty concerns the location of final authority within the territory: someone or some body must have the last word in law, and that authority can settle any dispute arising within the order, which is what allows a legal system to be a system rather than a series of unresolved conflicts. External sovereignty concerns the State’s standing among other States: it is equal to them in international law, subject to no superior except obligations it has itself accepted by treaty or custom, and its consent is what makes such obligations binding. The characteristics usually given are supremacy, because no authority stands above the sovereign in law; finality, because the sovereign settles what lower authorities cannot; indivisibility, because authority shared to the point of competing sovereigns ceases to be sovereignty; inalienability, because it cannot be surrendered without the State ceasing to be the same State; and absoluteness within its sphere, which means that no positive law imposed from outside limits it, even though its own constitution, morality and prudence may. Colonial rule shows the two kinds separating: a colony may have internal administration while external authority rests elsewhere. A strong answer therefore defines, lists the characteristics with explanation, and keeps the two kinds distinct throughout.
questions.explanation: Full marks need the definition, all five characteristics explained, and the internal/external distinction illustrated by a case where they separate.

questions.prompt: Is sovereignty a useful concept for understanding the modern state, or has pluralism and international integration made it obsolete?
questions.answer: The case for obsolescence begins with the pluralist evidence that authority in a modern society is distributed: churches, trade unions, professional bodies and international organisations all make binding rules, individuals owe obligations to several of them, and the state increasingly obtains much of its law and many of its limits from supranational institutions. Laski’s point that obligation is relative to function fits a world in which a person may be bound by domestic law, treaty-derived law and organisational rules simultaneously, and within the state the constitutional conventions and judicial review that constrain government make unlimited power a fiction in practice. The case for retention is stronger where it counts. However dispersed influence becomes, some institution must in the last resort be able to settle a constitutional dispute finally, and the state alone retains the powers to tax, legislate, conscript and enforce judgment, none of which any association or international body can exercise independently of state machinery. Treaty obligations are accepted by the state itself and can be denounced, so external commitments do not abolish external sovereignty; international organisations act through the consent of their members, as the history of the United Nations makes plain. The most defensible position is therefore conceptual narrowing rather than abandonment: sovereignty is obsolete as a claim to unlimited power, since no serious writer defends that, but indispensable as the concept of legal finality, because without it the question of who settles disputes has no answer. The modern work of the concept lies precisely in tracing where final authority now sits in a world of federations, unions and rights charters — which is a harder question, not an obsolete one.
questions.explanation: Full marks require the pluralist and integration evidence engaged seriously, the last-resort argument answered, and a judgement that distinguishes sovereignty as unlimited power from sovereignty as legal finality.
